# Git Flow: The Classic Model

After this page you can name Git Flow’s long-lived branches and when the extra machinery is worth it.

## The picture

```text
main          production; tagged releases
develop       next release; features merge here
feat/…        branched from develop, merged back (often --no-ff)
release/x.y   branched from develop, hotfixes, then merge to main *and* develop
hotfix/…      branched from main, merge to main *and* develop
```

`main` is always what is in production. `develop` is the integration line. Features never commit straight to `main`.

```text
 main     A ─────────────── H1 ── v1.2
            \             ↗
 develop     B ← C ← D ← E ← F
                  \     ↗
 feat/invoices      X ← Y
```

## Commands (shape, not a plugin)

```bash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git switch -c develop
git switch -c feat/invoices develop
# … commits …
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feat/invoices
git branch -d feat/invoices
```

`--no-ff` keeps a join node so `git log --first-parent develop` lists features.

## What it costs

Two long-lived branches that **diverge**. Every hotfix is merged twice. Release branches exist for weeks. For `desk-api` with one or two people, this is a lot of graph.

## What it buys

A support team that must ship `1.2.3` while `develop` already contains `2.0` work. Multiple versions in the wild. A release manager.

Use Git Flow when you **actually** have that. The original `git-flow` CLI is optional; the branch names are the model.

Chapter 31 is how a forge **enforces** this (protected `main`, required PRs). This page is the topology.
